### Clinical Relevance
Biomechanics is the reason behind most problems a replaced hip brings back to clinic.

#### Why the Surgeon Needs It
- Every unexplained finding has a biomechanical cause (Prof Gobba)
- Examples: no 28 mm head on the shelf, a leg turned in, a new limp, night pain on the side
- So a complaining patient is not blamed: the cause is found
- THA parts must survive years of cyclic loading of at least **3×** body weight (Campbell)
- Plates and nails share the load only until union; a THA carries it for life

#### The Six Topics
- Forces and offset are this chapter
- Version, range of motion and stability → 13 Instability
- Templating → 05 Planning

### Lever and Seesaw Principles
Two everyday machines explain all the forces around the hip.

#### The Door and Its Hinge
- Push a door far from its hinge and little force opens it
- Push near the hinge and you need much more force
[[FIG: Fig 3.1 · 3.1

#### The Seesaw
- The hip is the **fulcrum** of a seesaw, with a load on each side
- Light loads on both sides spare the hinge; heavy loads break it
- Balance needs equal **moments**, not equal forces
- **Torque** (moment) = force × its lever arm
- So 200 N balances 400 N when it sits at double the distance (Handbook)

### Single-Leg Stance
On one leg the pelvis has a single support, so the analysis starts there.

#### Double Stance
- In double stance, body weight is shared by both hips
[[FIG: Fig 3.2 · 3.1
- Lifting one leg changes the loading completely

#### Forces Tilting the Pelvis
- **W** is **5/6 of body weight**: the stance leg below the hip is excluded (Handbook)
- W pulls the free side down, so the pelvis wants to **drop**
- A visible drop is a **positive Trendelenburg sign**
- The **abductors** of the stance side pull back and keep it level

#### Role in Gait
- Single stance fills **half the gait cycle**
- In stance the abductors act from insertion to origin

### Lever Arms of Body Weight and Abductors
The pelvis behaves like a seesaw, so two moments must balance.

#### Definitions of the Lever Arms
| Symbol | What it is |
|---|---|
| **W** | body weight, 5/6 of the total |
| **B** | lever of W: body's centre of gravity to the hip centre |
| **M** | abductor force |
| **A** | lever of M: lateral greater trochanter to the hip centre |

- Prof Gobba's slides letter it **A × B = C × D**: A abductor force, C body weight

#### The Balance Equation
- At balance **W × B = M × A**, so **M = W × (B / A)**
- A long B or a short A makes the abductors work harder
- B is longer than A, so the abductors pull more than body weight
- The abductors pull ≈30° from vertical, so true force = vertical force / cos 30° (Handbook)

#### The Arthritic Hip
- Here the B : A ratio may reach **4 : 1** (Campbell)
- Head loss or a short neck shortens the abductor arm
- So does a posterior trochanter (external rotation deformity) and **DDH**

MEMORY HOOK — the bucket at arm's length
- A bucket at arm's length, gripped near the shoulder: that is the abductors' job, ≈2.5× body weight.

PITFALL — B ≈ 2A or 2.5A?
- The Handbook says B ≈ **2A** (M ≈ 2×); its cane example uses B/A = **3**
- Campbell says **2.5 : 1**, with JRF **3×** body weight
- Say → "Lever ratio ≈2.5, so abductors 2.5× and JRF ≈3× body weight (Campbell)."

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what decides the load on a hip?"
- "JRF depends on **W** and **M**: more weight or more muscle force, more load."
- "Raised by obesity, female pelvis, lateralised cup and low femoral offset."

### Definition
The JRF is the floor pushing back on the seesaw at its pivot.

#### Concept
- **JRF** is the sum of all forces acting across the hip, whatever their direction
- The hip is the **fulcrum** of the seesaw, so it carries both W and M
- It pushes back equally, by **Newton's third law**
[[FIG: Fig 3.4 · 3.2

#### Clinical Significance
- A high JRF speeds **prosthesis wear**
- In a native hip it speeds **degeneration**
- Excess weight and activity add to the forces that loosen, bend or break a stem

### Magnitude in Daily Activities
The textbook number is 3×, but the real load depends on what the patient is doing.

| Activity | Load on the head |
|---|---|
| **Single stance, walking** | ≈3× body weight (Campbell's estimate) |
| **Straight-leg raising** | about the same as stance |
| **Gait, calculated peak** | 3.5–5.0×; up to 6× in single stance |
| **Gait, measured in instrumented hips** | 2.6–3.0× |
| **Lifting, running, jumping** | up to **10×** |

- All figures in this table are from Campbell

### Out-of-Plane and Torsional Forces
The hip is loaded from the front as well as from above, and this twists the stem.

#### Sagittal-Plane Forces
- The centre of gravity is midline, anterior to S2, but **posterior** to the hip axis
- So sagittal forces bend the stem **posteriorly**
[[FIG: Fig 3.5 · 3.2
- They rise with the hip flexed: rising from a chair, stairs, inclines and lifting

#### Direction on the Head
- In gait the force meets the head **15–25°** anterior to the stem's sagittal plane
- On stairs and in straight-leg raising it acts even farther anterior
- So the stem is pushed into **retroversion**; these forces measure **0.6–0.9×** body weight

#### Torsion
- Coronal and sagittal forces together **twist** the stem (Campbell)
- So a cementless stem must be rotationally stable at once
- A cemented stem needs a shape that is rotationally stable in its mantle

### Factors Increasing the Joint Reaction Force
Anything that adds weight, lengthens B or shortens A pushes M up, and the JRF follows.

| Factor | Why it raises JRF |
|---|---|
| **Obesity** | more W |
| **Female** | wider pelvis, so a longer B |
| **Lateralised cup** | longer B; abductors stretched (more stable) but more wear |
| **Low femoral offset** | shorter A, because axis-to-trochanter length is fixed |
| **Load in the opposite hand** | adds to the B-side moment |

- A load carried in the **same-side** hand lowers the JRF instead
- If B = 3A, 100 N of weight needs 300 N of abductor force, not 200 N (Handbook)

MEMORY HOOK — the four Fs
- **F**at, **F**emale, **F**ar-out cup, **F**allen offset: the four Fs that raise the JRF.

### Factors Decreasing the Joint Reaction Force
Turn each cause around and you have the treatment.

#### Patient Measures
- **Lose weight**: each unit lost removes several units of hip load
- Use a **cane in the opposite hand** → 03.5

#### Surgical Measures
- Put the cup at the **anatomical centre**, medial and inferior: this gives the shortest B
- **Restore femoral offset**, so A is long again → 03.3

#### The Hip Centre
- The JRF is lowest with the hip centre at its **anatomic** site (Campbell)
- A **superior and lateral** or a **posterior** centre raises it
- **Isolated superior** placement adds little stress and finds viable bone in dysplasia or revision
- But non-anatomic centres show more radiolucency and migration in clinical series
- In dysplasia a **high hip centre** does well early (Prof Youness)
- But the long-term stress leads to **failure**
[[FIG: Fig 3.6 · 3.2

3.3.t: Offset, Centre of Rotation and Abductor Tension
3.3.b:
Now the surgeon's side: a THA can lengthen or shorten both levers.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does a THA change the levers?"
- "A **medialised cup** shortens B; more **femoral offset** lengthens A."
- "Muscle force depends on fibre stretch, so a slack abductor is a weak one."
- "Restore the centre of rotation, offset and leg length, so the abductors sit at resting length."

### Surgical Alteration of the Lever Arms
The cup sets B, and the femoral side sets A.

#### The Charnley Concept
- Charnley deepened the acetabulum to shorten B (Campbell)
- He reattached the osteotomised trochanter laterally to lengthen A
- Bringing B : A toward **1 : 1** cuts total hip load by **30%**, in theory

#### Medialisation and Offset
- Medialising the cup brings the hip centre toward the body weight line, so B shortens
- Increasing **femoral offset** moves the trochanter away from the hip centre, so A lengthens
- Either change means less abductor force for the same W
[[FIG: Fig 3.7 · 3.3
- Medialisation gains less in hips with more femoral anteversion (Terrier)

#### Current Practice
- Today medialisation is **not emphasised**: subchondral bone is kept
- The acetabulum is reamed only enough to cover the cup
- The trochanter is rarely osteotomised, so **offset** is the lever used now
- Plan the cup at its own level, not medialised or lateralised (Prof Fawzy)

#### The Trade-Off of a Lateral Cup
- A **lateralised cup** lengthens B, so it raises the JRF
- But it pushes head and trochanter outward, so the abductors are stretched

### Centre of Rotation and Offset Restoration
The levers work only if the new hip turns about the old centre.

#### Restoring the Centre of Rotation
- Restore the **centre of rotation** first (Prof Youness)
- It decides early results and how long the implant lasts
- The femoral side then restores offset, the abductor mechanism and limb length

#### Horizontal and Vertical Offset
- Restore both **horizontal** and **vertical** offset with the centre (Prof Fawzy)
[[FIG: Fig 3.8 · 3.3
- Missing them leaves the tissues lax, and the hip may dislocate
- Lax tissue then tempts a longer leg for stability, and a long leg is an unhappy patient
- Planning chooses a standard or a high-offset stem

#### Leg-Length Inequality and the Levers
- Leg-length inequality strains the abductors and shortens their lever arm (Prof Fawzy)
- So the abductors pull harder, and the JRF rises
- In the long term this means loosening and wear

### Length–Tension Principle
Lever length is half the story; the muscle must also be at the right stretch.

#### Principle
- The **length–tension principle**: muscle force depends on fibre stretch
- The Handbook calls it "Frank-Starling"; the skeletal-muscle name is length–tension
- So a slack abductor is a weak abductor

MEMORY HOOK — the slack bowstring
- A slack bowstring fires no arrow: restore the offset, and the abductors are strung again.

#### Femoral Offset
- **Offset** is the distance from the head centre to the femoral axis
- Only **neck length** and **neck–shaft angle** change it (Handbook)

#### Methods of Tensioning the Abductors
| Lever | How it works | Changes femoral offset? |
|---|---|---|
| **More femoral offset** | longer neck or lower neck–shaft angle → trochanter moves away from the hip centre | yes |
| **Trochanter transfer** | distal–lateral advancement stretches the gluteal fibres | no |
| **More acetabular offset** | lateralised cup → head and trochanter move outward | no |

PITFALL — "trochanteric transfer increases the offset"
- Transfer and a lateral cup stretch the abductors like offset, but leave femoral offset unchanged
- Say → "Only neck length and neck–shaft angle change femoral offset; the others only add tension."

### Clinical Application
The practical side of tension belongs to other chapters.
- Too little or too much offset, the shuck test, leg-length trade → 13 Instability
- Neck cut, leg length and templating the offset → 05 Planning

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is a Trendelenburg lurch?"
- "The trunk leans over the weak hip, so B shortens and the abductors need less force."
- "The **lurch** is compensation that works; it costs energy and looks like a limp."
- "The **Trendelenburg sign** is compensation that failed: the pelvis drops."

### Hip Abductor Muscles
The abductor group shares one nerve.
- The abductors are **gluteus medius**, **gluteus minimus** and **TFL** (tensor fasciae latae)
- All three are supplied by the **superior gluteal nerve**
- How surgery injures nerve and muscle → 13 Instability

### Trendelenburg Lurch and Trendelenburg Sign
The lurch and the sign sit on either side of the same failure.

#### Loss of Balance
- Destroyed abductors, as after a careless lateral approach, break A × B = C × D (Prof Gobba)
- Weight cannot drop overnight, so the patient shortens D, the body-weight arm

#### Trendelenburg Lurch
- The trunk shifts over the weak side, and the centre of gravity moves with it
- The trunk is centred over its new base of support
- So **B shortens**, even below A, and the weak abductors need less force (Handbook)
- The price is energy, and the gait looks like a limp
- The patient says, "I limp whenever I walk": a **Trendelenburg gait**

#### Trendelenburg Sign
- The abductors cannot hold the pelvis, so the free side **drops**

MEMORY HOOK — the clever cheat
- The lurch is a cheat that works; the Trendelenburg sign is the cheat caught out: the pelvis drops.

PITFALL — every short stance is not weak abductors
- An **antalgic** gait also shortens stance, so it can look the same
- Say → "I test abductor power directly before I call it a Trendelenburg gait."

3.5.b:
A cane fights the same lever from the other side, so it can do the abductors' work.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why does a cane help an arthritic hip?"
- "A cane in the **opposite** hand has a long lever **C**, giving a counter-torque."
- "So abductor force falls, and with it the JRF, pain and wear."
- "**15%** of body weight on the cane **halves** the abductor force."

### Cane Moment Equation
The cane adds a second moment on the abductor side.

#### The Equation
- **W × B = (M × A) + (R × C)**
- **R** is the cane force; **C** is the cane's lever arm from the hip
- With the cane the equation balances, so the patient need not lean
[[FIG: Fig 3.9 · 3.5
- A lower M means a lower JRF, so less pain, degeneration and wear

#### Choice of Hand
- The **opposite hand** gives the longest C
- In the same-side hand the cane has almost no lever arm
- It does no harm there, but its effect is weak (Handbook)

MEMORY HOOK — fifteen buys fifty
- **15%** on an opposite-hand cane, **50%** less abductor work: fifteen buys fifty.

### Worked Example
The numbers show why a little weight on a long lever goes a long way.

| Step | Numbers | Abductor force M |
|---|---|---|
| **No cane** | W 100 N, B 15 cm, A 5 cm → 100 × 15 / 5 | **300 N** |
| **Cane, 15%** | R 15 N, C 50 cm → 1500 = 5M + 750 | **150 N** |

- So **15%** on an opposite cane cuts abductor force by **50%** (Handbook)
- W stays at 100 N in the example, which is a simplification

### Correct Use
A cane helps only if it is the right height and moves at the right time.
- Set the handle at the **wrist crease**
- Move the cane **with the affected leg**, then step with the good leg

#### Choice of Hand
- The **opposite hand** gives the longest C

MEMORY HOOK — fifteen buys fifty
- **15%** on an opposite-hand cane, **50%** less abductor work: fifteen buys fifty.

3.5.2.b:
The numbers show why a little weight on a long lever goes a long way.

| Step | Numbers | Abductor force M |
|---|---|---|
| **No cane** | W 100 N, B 15 cm, A 5 cm → 100 × 15 / 5 | **300 N** |
| **Cane, 15%** | R 15 N, C 50 cm → 1500 = 5M + 750 | **150 N** |

- So **15%** on an opposite cane cuts abductor force by **50%** (Handbook)
- W stays at 100 N in the example, which is a simplification

3.5.3.b:
A cane helps only if it is the right height and moves at the right time.
- Set the handle at the **wrist crease**
- Move the cane **with the affected leg**, then step with the good leg
